  1. Fix FreeCAD and fill it with engineering grade, sigma six certified plugins for analysis. Bring on the engineers!

  5. A complete application fully dedicated to reading data and creating charts that can be exported in a variety of formats. I currently make my charts using MATLAB or Python, but most users can't handle that and honestly its a pain in the ass.

  6. Battlefield 4: FOSS edition with options for hosting your own server.

  7. A super-driver framework that magically makes all the Bluetooth, Ethernet, and WiFi components work well in a truly free-as-in-freedom open source way.

  8. A FOSS DRM content-management framework based on key cryptography that allows people like Netflix and Amazon to stream their content to paying customers on Linux. The existing implementations aren't so great for us.

Make Krita or GIMP as good as Photoshop. Honestly, I think its already there, but the professionals disagree with me.

For general use, GIMP is perfectly fine. I can't speak for other professions, but I was in the print industry (digital prepress) for about a decade. The main problems with GIMP for professional printing:

  1. No PANTONE colors. Pantone licensing is expensive so it will never be included into the GIMP.
  2. Poor CMYK support. The majority of color printing is actually spot color (black plus one color, generally the plus one color is a pantone color) the rest of the full-color is generally CMYK printing. There's also CMYK plus spot, but it's used rarely because it's expensive to print.
    • GIMP does support CMYK separations with GEGL, but it's fucking painful to use.
    • Most print shops can put in curves and convert RGB images to CMYK, but it's gonna cause the colors to shift. It generally adds 15% black to the images. If you have more than a handful of customers, adding all of those different color corrective curves to fix their RGB -> CMYK quickly becomes cumbersome. Even when you explain it to customers, they just know that their version of blue doesn't match what came off of the press.
  3. Never bothered me, but co-workers really hate the different keyboard shortcuts. Hit 'M' for the marquee tool, nope, that's the move tool. Hit 'B' for the paint brush, nope, that's the path tool. There's a way to get you GIMP shortcuts pretty close to photoshop, but most people don't want to fool with it. Especially if they have access to Photoshop already.

1. Pantone is a proprietary standard. We would need an open source equivalent, or we would need to bribe Pantone to be more cross-platform.

  2. Krita supports CMYK correctly. GIMP does not. With GIMP the user is likely to accidentally convert through RGB back to CMYK without warning. Its just a mess.

  3. There really ought to be more effort from Krita and GIMP to mimic photoshop. That's the market they need to capture. If nothing else, there should be "keyboard shortcut profile" files you can download, and the photoshop equivalent should come standard.

I feel your pain, I really do. From a technical perspective photoshop has a clear lead. Photoshop also has more plugins than GIMP and KRITA have combined.
